prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Robert Swan's life reads like a boy's own adventure tale with a modern eco-twist. Robert Swan was the first man to walk to both the North and South Poles. Inspired by the daring age of Antarctic exploration, Swan followed in the footsteps of his heroes; the men who risked, and lost, their lives to reach the South Pole. At the age of 29 he embarked on an expedition to the South Pole that was unsupported -- a trek that required him to pull his own sleigh and that lacked medical support crews. By the time he was 33 he had become the first man to walk to both the North and South poles unsupported. But for Swan, the epic journeys to the Poles, and the sailing and overland adventures that have followed, unearthed more than just a spirit for adventure. He experienced firsthand the impact of humanity on the environment when under the hole in the ozone layer at the South Pole, the harsh ultraviolet rays from the sun burned his skin and permanently changed the color of his eyes. It firmed a desire to preserve the fragile natural world and to educate and inspire others, particularly the next generation of decision-makers to do the same. "As the last unspoiled wilderness on Earth, Antarctica is currently protected by the treaty prohibiting drilling and mining until 2041. Decisions made by today's youth will impact our entire planet's ecosystem and the future of life on earth," he says on 2041.com. His polar icewalks gained international attention and in 1992 he was asked to speak at the UN Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro, later gaining an OBE and being appointed Special Envoy to the Director General of UNESCO in recognition of his work. At the Earth Summit in Rio he committed to a "global mission" to remove 1,500 tons of waste from Antarctica. Swan and a team of young people from across the world were successful in cleaning up the Russian Antarctic base of Bellinghausen by 2000, making it inhabitable for wildlife again. Foresight, planning and determination then are not alien to a man who spent five years sourcing the funding for his first Antarctic expedition, and Swan's latest project is taking an even longer-term view. Swan founded his organization "2041" in 2003 in order to further his mission of action and education. Named after the year in which Antarctica's protection against mineral exploitation ends, Swan regularly takes business people, teachers and students on expeditions to Antarctica to impress on those with the capacity to enact change that preservation of the environment is essential and achievable. Continuing the green mission on the continent by minimizing the human footprint in the region, his international teams have helped design and build the world's first education station in Antarctica that is run solely on renewable energy. Add to the expeditions, ocean voyages on a boat with sails made from recycled plastic bottles, and it's clear that the veteran polar explorer is a man who is doing all he can to protect and preserve the Antarctic.

(CNN) -- Robert Swan’s life reads like a classic adventure tale with a modern environmental twist. He was the first man to walk to both the North and South Poles.

Inspired by the heroic age of Antarctic exploration, Swan followed in the footsteps of the men he admired—explorers who risked, and sometimes lost, their lives in pursuit of the South Pole. At the age of 29, he embarked on an unsupported expedition to the South Pole, pulling his own sledge without the assistance of medical support crews. By 33, he had become the first man to walk unsupported to both the North and South Poles.

For Swan, however, these epic polar journeys—and the sailing and overland adventures that followed—awakened more than a passion for exploration. He witnessed firsthand humanity’s impact on the environment. Beneath the hole in the ozone layer at the South Pole, intense ultraviolet radiation burned his skin and permanently changed the color of his eyes.

The experience strengthened his determination to preserve the fragile natural world and to educate and inspire others—particularly the next generation of decision-makers—to do the same.

“As the last unspoiled wilderness on Earth, Antarctica is currently protected by the treaty prohibiting drilling and mining until 2041. Decisions made by today’s youth will impact our entire planet’s ecosystem and the future of life on earth,” he says on 2041.com.

Swan’s polar ice walks attracted international attention, and in 1992 he was invited to speak at the United Nations Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro. He later received an OBE and was appointed Special Envoy to the Director-General of UNESCO in recognition of his work.

At the Rio Earth Summit, Swan committed to a “global mission” to remove 1,500 tons of waste from Antarctica. By 2000, he and a team of young people from around the world had successfully cleaned up the Russian Antarctic base at Bellingshausen, making the area habitable for wildlife once again.

Foresight, planning, and determination are hardly unfamiliar qualities to a man who spent five years securing funding for his first Antarctic expedition. Swan’s latest project, however, takes an even longer-term perspective.

In 2003, he founded his organization, “2041,” to advance his mission of action and education. Named for the year in which Antarctica’s protection from mineral exploitation ends, the organization regularly takes businesspeople, teachers, and students on expeditions to the continent. Swan’s aim is to demonstrate to those with the power to enact change that environmental preservation is both essential and achievable.

Continuing this green mission while minimizing humanity’s footprint on the continent, his international teams have helped design and build the world’s first Antarctic education station powered entirely by renewable energy.

With these expeditions and ocean voyages aboard a boat whose sails are made from recycled plastic bottles, it is clear that the veteran polar explorer is doing everything he can to protect and preserve Antarctica.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style profile of polar explorer and environmentalist Robert Swan, covering his unsupported journeys to both poles, the effect of ozone depletion on him, and his work protecting Antarctica through the organization 2041.
counterfactuals.output:
**Robert Swan’s polar journeys turned an explorer into an Antarctic advocate**

Robert Swan has spent much of his life measuring human endurance against the coldest places on Earth. But it was the sun — intensified by a thinning ozone layer — that helped transform the British explorer into an environmental campaigner.

In January 1986, Swan reached the South Pole after an approximately 900-mile journey across Antarctica with Roger Mear and Gareth Wood. The team traveled without motorized support, hauling its supplies on sledges and following the route associated with British explorer Robert Falcon Scott.

Three years later, Swan led the Icewalk expedition to the North Pole. The grueling trek across shifting sea ice made him the first person widely recognized as having walked to both geographic poles.

Those achievements came at a cost. During the Antarctic expedition, Swan and his teammates traveled beneath the ozone hole, where reduced atmospheric protection allowed stronger ultraviolet radiation to reach the surface. Swan has described suffering serious sun damage, including blistered skin and lasting changes to his eyes — an experience that made ozone depletion feel immediate rather than theoretical.

The expedition also taught him that Antarctica was not insulated from the rest of the world. Pollution generated thousands of miles away could still affect the continent, while warming temperatures and changing sea ice threatened polar ecosystems.

Swan later founded **2041**, an organization dedicated to protecting Antarctica and promoting renewable energy, conservation and environmental leadership. Its name points to what Swan has long presented as a crucial period for the international agreements governing the continent, when he believes the world must be prepared to defend Antarctica from commercial exploitation.

Through leadership programs and expeditions, 2041 has taken business executives, students, educators and policymakers to Antarctica, aiming to turn firsthand experience into action at home. Swan has also used renewable-energy projects and public speaking to argue that environmental protection must be paired with practical changes in technology and behavior.

His message is rooted in the extremes he witnessed: Antarctica may appear remote, but it is connected to decisions made everywhere.

For Swan, reaching the poles was never the final destination. The larger journey has been persuading others that the planet’s last great wilderness cannot protect itself.

**Robert Swan, OBE** is a British polar explorer, environmentalist, and founder of the **2041 Foundation**. He is best known as the first person to have walked to both the **South Pole** and **North Pole**:

- In **1985–86**, he led the *In the Footsteps of Scott* expedition to the South Pole.
- In **1989**, he reached the North Pole on foot.

Those journeys shaped his environmental work. In Antarctica, Swan and his teammates experienced unusually intense ultraviolet exposure associated with the ozone hole; later, in the Arctic, he saw unstable and melting sea ice. He came to view the polar regions not as remote wildernesses but as early-warning systems for global environmental damage.

After the expeditions, Swan shifted from exploration to advocacy. He:

- Founded what became the **2041 Foundation**, which promotes Antarctic protection, climate education, and renewable energy.
- Organized Antarctic expeditions for students, educators, and business leaders so they could witness climate impacts firsthand and become environmental advocates.
- Helped with efforts to remove waste from Antarctic research areas and demonstrated the use of renewable energy in extreme conditions.
- Campaigned against mineral exploitation and for continued international cooperation under the **Antarctic Treaty System**.

The name “2041” refers to the period when provisions of the Antarctic environmental regime could become eligible for review. It is often said that the Antarctic Treaty “expires” in 2041, but that is inaccurate: the treaty has no expiration date, and the mining ban under the Environmental Protocol cannot simply lapse automatically. Swan uses the date symbolically to encourage present-day leaders to ensure Antarctica remains protected for science and peace.

His central message is that personal experience of the poles gave him both evidence of environmental change and a platform to persuade governments, companies, and younger generations to preserve Antarctica.

# From the Poles to the Podium, Robert Swan Turned Exploration Into an Environmental Mission

Robert Swan’s most consequential journey may not have been the one that took him across Antarctica or over the shifting ice of the Arctic Ocean. It may have begun in Rio de Janeiro in 1992, when the British explorer appeared at the United Nations Earth Summit and recast a career built on polar endurance as a campaign for environmental action.

By then, Swan had already secured his place in exploration history. In January 1986, he reached the South Pole as part of the “In the Footsteps of Scott” expedition, which sought to echo the human-powered journey of British explorer Robert Falcon Scott. Three years later, Swan reached the North Pole with the Icewalk expedition, becoming the first person to walk to both geographic poles.

The two landscapes gave him different warnings. In Antarctica, Swan has said that exposure to intense ultraviolet radiation damaged his eyes and blistered his face—an experience he associated with depletion of the ozone layer. In the Arctic, his team encountered unstable, thinning sea ice that could fracture and drift beneath them.

Those experiences shaped the message Swan carried to the 1992 Earth Summit, the landmark gathering where governments negotiated major agreements on climate change, biodiversity and sustainable development. His appearance placed the explorer among political leaders, scientists and campaigners trying to turn environmental concern into international policy.

For Swan, the summit also marked a shift from witnessing environmental damage to trying to repair it.

One of his most ambitious projects focused on Bellingshausen Station, Russia’s Antarctic research base on King George Island. Like a number of older polar installations, the area had accumulated abandoned machinery, fuel drums, scrap metal and other waste from decades of activity in a place where disposal and removal are exceptionally difficult.

Swan helped organize an international cleanup effort that brought together young volunteers and specialists. Over several seasons, the project removed and prepared large quantities of debris for recycling or safe disposal outside Antarctica. Reports associated with the campaign have put the total at roughly 1,500 tonnes.

The operation was more than a logistical exercise. It was intended as a demonstration that responsibility for Antarctica did not end with scientific discovery or heroic travel. The continent, Swan argued through his work, could not be treated as both a symbol of pristine nature and a dumping ground.

That idea later became central to 2041, the organization he founded to educate young people and business leaders about climate change, conservation and renewable energy. Its name refers to the year when the Antarctic Treaty’s environmental protocol can become eligible for review under specified conditions—a date Swan uses to emphasize the need for continued protection of the continent.

Through expeditions, leadership programs and public speaking, Swan has taken students, educators and corporate participants to Antarctica, using the setting as an open-air classroom. The programs connect the fate of the polar regions with decisions made far away: how electricity is generated, how buildings are heated, how waste is handled and how companies use resources.

At Bellingshausen, that educational mission took physical form in the E-Base, a small Antarctic facility designed to operate with renewable power, including wind and solar energy. Swan used the project to show that cleaner technologies could function even in one of the world’s most demanding environments. The larger argument was deliberately practical: if renewable systems could work in Antarctica, they could be adopted in schools, offices and communities elsewhere.

His initiatives have continued to stress what he calls action at the local level—moving beyond concern about melting ice and rising temperatures to measurable changes in energy use. Participants in his programs are encouraged to return home with projects of their own, turning an Antarctic experience into work on efficiency, renewable power, waste reduction or climate education.

Swan’s career has therefore followed an unusual arc. The early expeditions were tests of endurance, dependent on planning, teamwork and the willingness to keep moving through danger. The later campaigns applied much the same philosophy to environmental problems.

The poles made him famous. The Earth Summit gave him a larger platform. Bellingshausen offered a chance to replace rhetoric with cleanup work, while his renewable-energy programs turned Antarctica into a lesson about choices made everywhere else.

For Swan, the frozen continent is no longer simply a destination to be reached. It is a warning—and a classroom.

counterfactuals.output:
Robert Swan, the first person to walk to both the North and South Poles, created the **2041 Foundation** to motivate emerging leaders—young professionals, entrepreneurs, policymakers, and educators—to become advocates for Antarctica.

His approach is to:

- take future decision-makers on Antarctic expeditions so they experience the continent’s fragility firsthand;
- teach leadership, climate science, conservation, and renewable-energy practices;
- encourage participants to influence governments, businesses, and communities; and
- build public support for keeping Antarctica protected from mineral exploitation.

The name **“2041”** reflects Swan’s warning that Antarctica’s protections could face political pressure or reconsideration around that period. However, the legal situation is often simplified: the Antarctic Treaty itself does **not** expire in 2041. The Madrid Protocol bans mineral-resource activities other than scientific research, and its review procedure can first be invoked in **2048**—even then, mining would not automatically become legal.

Swan’s broader mission is therefore preventive: create a generation of influential leaders well before any future review, so that Antarctica continues to be treated as a natural reserve devoted to peace and science rather than as a source of oil, gas, or minerals.

# Robert Swan: From Polar Pioneer to Protector of the Planet

When Robert Swan reached the North Pole in 1989, he completed a feat no person had achieved before: travelling on foot, without outside support, to both the North and South Poles. Yet the most important outcome of those journeys was not the record itself. It was the realization that the world’s most remote places were already being transformed by human activity.

Swan had set out to become an explorer. He returned as an environmental campaigner.

## A childhood ambition at the edge of the world

Inspired by the great polar expeditions of Robert Falcon Scott and Ernest Shackleton, Swan dreamed from an early age of Antarctica. That ambition eventually became a demanding 900-mile journey to the South Pole, completed in 1986 with teammates Roger Mear and Gareth Wood.

The expedition was deliberately austere. The men hauled their supplies across the ice, facing violent winds, extreme cold and the exhausting monotony of a landscape in which every horizon seemed impossibly distant. There was little margin for error. Survival depended on discipline, teamwork and the willingness to continue when progress was measured in painful steps.

But Antarctica revealed more than Swan had expected. His team experienced the effects associated with the thinning ozone layer, including intense exposure to ultraviolet radiation. In a place that appeared pristine and untouched, he encountered evidence that pollution produced thousands of miles away could still leave a mark.

Three years later, Swan reached the North Pole after another gruelling unsupported journey. There, the danger was different. The Arctic Ocean was not a fixed white continent but a shifting, breaking surface of sea ice. Cracks could open without warning, and the ice moved beneath the expeditioners’ feet.

At opposite ends of the Earth, Swan saw the same truth: remoteness offered no protection from global environmental change.

## The end of one journey—and the beginning of another

Many explorers spend their lives seeking the next summit, crossing or record. Swan chose a different path. Having reached both poles, he began using his experience to connect environmental science with human emotion.

His message was simple: people protect what they understand, and they understand most deeply what they have experienced.

Swan became a prominent advocate for Antarctica, speaking to governments, businesses, schools and international organizations. He founded the 2041 Foundation, named for the year often associated with the earliest possible review process concerning key provisions of the Antarctic environmental regime. The foundation’s purpose is to build support for keeping Antarctica protected and dedicated to peace and science.

Rather than treating environmentalism as a matter only for researchers or policymakers, Swan sought to develop new generations of leaders. Through expeditions and educational programs, he brought young people, entrepreneurs, teachers and executives to Antarctica so they could witness its scale, beauty and fragility for themselves.

The aim was not tourism for its own sake. It was transformation.

## Turning exploration into responsibility

Swan’s evolution reflects a broader change in the meaning of exploration. Earlier generations often set out to conquer blank spaces on maps. Today, the greater challenge is to preserve the living systems those maps contain.

For Swan, endurance became a tool for advocacy. The authority he earned on the ice allowed him to speak credibly about climate change, renewable energy and long-term stewardship. He also worked to demonstrate that expeditions could reduce their environmental footprint, using cleaner technologies and renewable power where possible.

His campaigns have emphasized an essential point: Antarctica may belong to no single country, but responsibility for its future belongs to everyone.

The continent helps regulate the global climate, stores immense quantities of freshwater and supports ecosystems linked to oceans around the world. What happens there will not remain there. Changes in polar ice affect sea levels, weather patterns and communities far beyond the frozen south.

## A different kind of courage

Walking to the poles required physical courage—the ability to withstand cold, hunger, exhaustion and fear. Environmental campaigning required another kind: the courage to challenge short-term thinking and to ask institutions and individuals to act for a future they may never personally see.

That second journey is less dramatic than hauling a sledge across a blizzard, but it may be more consequential.

Robert Swan’s story reminds us that achievement is not only about reaching a destination. It is also about what we do with the perspective gained along the way. He went to the ends of the Earth seeking adventure and returned with a mission: to ensure that those places remain wild, protected and capable of inspiring generations yet to come.

His greatest expedition, in other words, did not end at either pole. It began there.
